anchor_text: we came in with Richard Conqueror
summary: Sly mangles history by fusing 'William the Conqueror' — who invaded England from Normandy in 1066 — with 'Richard,' probably meaning Richard I (Coeur-de-lion). The blunder is the joke: Sly claims ancient Norman lineage to defend his dignity while getting the name completely wrong.
detail: The historical reference in Sly's mind is almost certainly to William I, who conquered England at the Battle of Hastings in 1066. Confusing him with 'Richard' may be a dim memory of Richard I (reigned 1189-99), who was similarly a Norman. The claim to have 'come in with the Conqueror' was a proverbial Elizabethan boast of ancient English family; applied to the itinerant tinker Sly, whose family is unknown, it is self-deflating comedy. It also establishes immediately that Sly's pretensions outrun his knowledge, a theme the Lord's trick will exploit.

anchor_text: paucas pallabris; let the world slide. Sessa
summary: 'Paucas pallabris' is a garbling of the Spanish phrase 'pocas palabras,' meaning 'few words' — i.e., 'enough said.' 'Sessa' is an untranslatable exclamation, possibly from the French 'cessez' (stop), used as a call to be quiet or give up. Both were catch-phrases associated with low comedy and popular plays.
detail: The phrase 'pocas palabras' (Spanish for 'few words, say no more') was in circulation on the Elizabethan stage as stage-foreign comic slang; Sly has picked up a half-understood phrase from popular entertainment. 'Sessa' or 'ceese' appears in several contemporary plays and may derive from the French 'cessez.' Both expressions appear again in King Lear 3.4, where Edgar uses 'sesey' in his mad-Tom disguise, suggesting they belonged to a repertoire of stage low-life patter. The mixing of Spanish and pseudo-French in a tinker's mouth reinforces that Sly is performing a bluster he has absorbed from shows — appropriate in an Induction built around theatrical performance.

anchor_text: Go by, Saint Jeronimy, go to thy cold bed and warm thee
summary: Sly is mangling a line from Thomas Kyd's hugely popular revenge play The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587), in which the mad old man Hieronimo cries 'Go by, go by.' The play was so well known in the 1590s that its catch-phrases were the comedy of the day. 'Saint Jeronimy' conflates the saint Jerome with the character's name Hieronimo.
detail: Kyd's Spanish Tragedy was one of the biggest hits of the Elizabethan stage, and Hieronimo's ravings became a byword for theatrical excess. The phrase 'Go by, Hieronimo' and its variants were both earnest theatrical currency and targets of parody; Ben Jonson mocked audiences who still called for it as old-fashioned in the early 1600s. Sly's garbling of the quotation — giving it to a saint and adding the cold-bed tag — shows him parroting theatrical fashion without quite remembering it, which is another joke at his expense. It also grounds the Induction in the actual theatrical culture of the 1590s: we are watching a play about watching plays.

anchor_text: fetch the third-borough
summary: A 'third-borough' (also 'thirdborough') was a minor parish officer, a kind of petty constable responsible for keeping the peace at the local level. The Hostess is threatening to fetch the law — the closest equivalent to calling the police.
detail: The office of thirdborough was a survival of Anglo-Saxon tithing-man law; by Shakespeare's time it was a low-level constabulary position in rural areas, effectively equivalent to the headborough or petty constable. Shakespeare uses similar figures comically in other plays: Dogberry in Much Ado About Nothing is the stock bumbling version of this kind of parish law officer. Sly's breezy reply — 'Third, or fourth, or fifth borough, I'll answer him by law' — shows he is either drunk enough to welcome a legal fight or, more likely, drunk enough not to care.

anchor_text: how like a swine he lies! Grim death, how foul and loathsome is thine image
summary: The Lord apostrophizes Death directly — 'Grim death, how foul and loathsome is thine image' — treating the insensible, snoring Sly as a living portrait of what a corpse looks like. The figure is apostrophe (addressing an abstraction as a person) and memento mori (a reminder that death waits for everyone). The irony is that Sly's 'death' is entirely self-inflicted by alcohol.
detail: The memento mori — literally 'remember you must die' — was a standard moralizing topos in Elizabethan visual culture and literature; skulls, hourglasses, and sleeping figures served as emblems of death's imminence. The Lord's exclamation literalizes the emblem: a sleeping drunk becomes a walking vanitas. Shakespeare uses the same conceit at length in Hamlet (the graveyard scene, Yorick's skull). The swine comparison also carries a moral weight — 'swine' was shorthand for gluttony and bestial appetite (the sin Sly embodies) — making his image not just of death but of degraded, animal death. The whole speech sets up the Lord's 'jest' as something like a theatrical experiment: can a man be restored to dignity by being treated with dignity?

anchor_text: I will practise on this drunken man
summary: The Lord's plan — dressing a sleeping beggar as a nobleman and convincing him he has woken from a long madness — enacts a traditional story known as 'the sleeper awakened.' A similar trick was reportedly played by Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy (d. 1467), and a version circulates in the Arabian Nights. The whole play-within-a-play that follows is staged as entertainment for this gulled tinker.
detail: The motif of a sleeping commoner or fool woken into false lordship, then returned to his old life confused about which was the dream, is one of the most widespread joke-stories in European and Near Eastern tradition. An early version attributed to Philip of Burgundy was recorded in the Tudor period and has since been traced to the Arabian Nights tale 'The Sleeper Awakened.' In the Folio text of The Taming of the Shrew the frame is never closed — Sly disappears after Induction 2 and is never shown being undeceived. In the related anonymous play The Taming of A Shrew (1594) the frame is completed, with Sly sent home still claiming to know how to tame a wife from what he dreamed. The open frame of the Folio text leaves teasing questions about reality and performance that resonate through the main play's disguises.

anchor_text: hang it round with all my wanton pictures
summary: 'Wanton pictures' are erotic or sensually suggestive paintings — specifically, as Induction 2 reveals, paintings of classical myths from Ovid: Venus and Adonis, Io seduced by Jove, Daphne fleeing Apollo. These hung in noble houses as legitimate art, but their subjects were conventional occasions for depicting undress and pursuit. They are part of the luxury the Lord will use to trick Sly into believing he is a wealthy man.
detail: In Induction 2 the servants offer Sly three specific paintings drawn from Ovid's Metamorphoses: Adonis by a brook with 'Cytherea all in sedges hid,' Io 'beguiled' by Jove, and Daphne running through a thorny wood. All three are standard subjects of the European Renaissance art tradition — Titian, Veronese, and many others painted exactly these myths for wealthy patrons. The word 'wanton' does not mean pornographic but 'lascivious, playful, amorous' — appropriate for Ovidian erotic myth. The Lord's gallery doubles as a practical joke prop (to awe Sly with luxury) and as an advertisement of the comedy's own Ovidian palette.

anchor_text: I think 'twas Soto that your honour means
summary: The Player names the role he played as 'Soto' — generally identified with a character of that name in John Fletcher's play Women Pleased (written c. 1620). Because the 1623 Folio was probably set from a playing-text in use around 1620-23, this looks less like a rare early allusion than evidence of a later theatrical touch-up by the King's Men. Editors have debated whether the line is an interpolation.
detail: The name 'Soto' is not found in any surviving play that plausibly predates The Taming of the Shrew, but it matches a comic character in Fletcher's Women Pleased (written for the King's Men, c. 1620). The Folio Shrew may therefore reflect a revision or interpolation made by the company around 1620-23, roughly thirty years after the play's original composition (c. 1590-92). The Lord's remembering a Player's role is a kind of in-house theatrical compliment — exactly the sort of allusion a company might update in revival.

anchor_text: see him dress'd in all suits like a lady
summary: The Lord's plan to dress his page Bartholomew as Sly's 'wife' is a joke that works on two levels: for the audience, it layers a real theatrical convention (boy actors playing women) inside a stage fiction about a boy playing a woman. All female roles in Elizabethan professional theatre were taken by boy apprentices or young male actors, so the audience would immediately see the comedy of a boy-plays-woman-fools-a-drunk.
detail: Elizabethan professional playing companies employed boy apprentices to play all female roles; no women appeared on the public stage in England until after the Restoration (1660). When the Lord instructs Bartholomew to 'do him obeisance' with 'soft low tongue and lowly courtesy' and hold himself like 'a gentlewoman,' he is giving the same instructions an experienced dramatist would give a boy actor. The meta-theatrical joke runs through the whole Induction: the page performing a wife for Sly mirrors the boy actor performing a wife for the audience, and the 'play' put on for Sly features boys playing all the Paduan women, including Katharine and Bianca. The instructions the Lord gives are unusually precise — the onion trick for tears (TLN 125-127) is a piece of practical stage craft, exactly what a director might tell a boy struggling to weep on cue.

anchor_text: a pot of small ale
summary: Small ale was weak, cheaply brewed beer, the everyday drink of the working poor; sack was a strong Spanish or Canary wine, an expensive luxury drink of the wealthy. The First Servant offers Sly sack, the drink of lords; Sly demands small ale, the drink of tinkers. The contrast in a single exchange flags the whole trick: Sly answers every aristocratic courtesy in the idiom of his real station.
detail: Sack (from Spanish seco, dry) was a fortified white wine imported from Spain or the Canary Islands, fashionable at the Elizabethan court and in wealthy households. Small ale had a low alcohol content and was brewed without hops; it cost a penny a pot and was standard on alehouse benches. Sly's dogged preference for it over sack is the first and recurring marker of his authentic voice against the servants' elaborate fiction.

anchor_text: I am Christophero Sly; call not me honour nor lordship
summary: Sly catalogues his true biography against the servants' flattery: a pedlar (travelling goods-seller), a card-maker (one who combs raw wool into fibres for spinning), a bear-herd (keeper of a performing bear, a common street entertainment), and now a tinker (an itinerant mender of pots and pans). Each occupation is a rung lower on the Elizabethan social ladder than the last. The list is both comic and sharp-eyed social observation.
detail: Card-making (carding wool) and tinker were trades so lowly they barely registered in guild records. Bear-wards or bear-herds led chained bears from town to town for the baiting-ring; they were licensed but disreputable, sharing the vagrant fringe with players. The Italian-inflected 'Christophero' is itself a small joke: Sly is no more an Italian lord than he is a tinker who is one.

anchor_text: the lustful bed / On purpose trimm'd up for Semiramis
summary: Semiramis was the legendary Assyrian queen, famous in classical tradition for extreme beauty, power, and unbounded sexual appetite. She was proverbial for luxury and lust. The Lord flatters Sly with a bed said to outshine even hers, implying a magnificence beyond all queens of the ancient world.
detail: The historical core is Sammu-ramat, an Assyrian queen-regent (c. 811-806 BCE), but the legendary Semiramis derives mainly from Diodorus Siculus (Library of History 2.4-20) and was transmitted through Boccaccio's De Mulieribus Claris and other compilations. She was said to have founded Babylon and its hanging gardens, led vast armies, and taken countless lovers. For Shakespeare's audience she was simply the type of a voluptuous, all-powerful queen. The phrase 'lustful bed' signals what makes her a useful comparison point: the luxury of the Lord's imaginary bed exceeds even this byword for carnal magnificence.

anchor_text: Io as she was a maid / And how she was beguiled and surpris'd
summary: Io was a priestess of Juno seduced by Jupiter, who wrapped the earth in a cloud to conceal the act from his wife; Juno, suspicious, came down and Jupiter transformed Io into a white cow. The painting shows the moment of the seduction — Io as a girl, 'beguiled and surpris'd.' The word 'beguiled' implies both deception and seduction, as the painting is 'as lively painted as the deed was done.'
detail: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.583-600, narrates Jupiter's cloud-trick ('as lively painted as the deed was done') and the transformation; Golding's 1567 English translation was well-known. The second of the trio of Ovidian paintings, this one stresses divine violation rather than mutual desire — Jupiter uses supernatural power to have his way. The detail 'as lively painted as the deed was done' is a connoisseur's phrase for trompe-l'oeil illusionism, the highest praise for Renaissance painting.

anchor_text: Daphne roaming through a thorny wood, / Scratching her legs
summary: Daphne was a nymph who fled the god Apollo's pursuit until she prayed for rescue and was transformed into a laurel tree. The servant's painting adds a grim painterly detail not in Ovid: Daphne's legs bleeding from the thorns as she runs, so realistically rendered that 'one shall swear she bleeds' and 'sad Apollo weep.' The third Ovidian painting (with Adonis and Io), all three from the Metamorphoses.
detail: Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.452-567 (Golding 1567), is the source; Shakespeare's bleeding-legs embellishment converts a narrative of metamorphosis into a painter's showpiece of pathos. Apollo's pursuit of Daphne arises from Cupid's revenge: Cupid shot Apollo with a gold arrow (of love) and Daphne with a lead arrow (of aversion), making the chase hopeless from the start. After her transformation Apollo made the laurel his sacred emblem and crowned poets with it — so the myth doubles as an origin story for the laurel wreath of literary fame.

anchor_text: teach you gamut in a briefer sort, / More pleasant, pithy, and effectual
summary: The 'gamut' was the complete musical scale as taught in Renaissance music theory, built on the Guidonian system of hexachords (six-note scales named with the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la). Each note had a letter name combined with a hexachord syllable: 'gamma ut' (G in the lowest octave, hence 'gamut') was the bottom of the system; 'A re,' 'B mi,' 'C fa ut,' 'D sol re,' 'E la mi' are the next notes in order — exactly what Bianca reads from Hortensio's paper (lines 1296-1301). Hortensio has set his wooing to the notation: 'Gamut I am, the ground of all accord' makes him the foundational G note (accord = harmony but also agreement/affection), and each subsequent syllable is a line of verse to Bianca. The scene's central joke is that the music lesson is itself a composed love-letter, the pedagogical frame indistinguishable from courtship. Bianca reads it aloud and dismisses it, preferring 'old fashions' — a miniature version of her eventual choice of Lucentio over Hortensio.

anchor_text: proclaim the banns
summary: The 'banns' (or 'banns of marriage') were a public announcement, read aloud in church on three successive Sundays before a wedding, naming the couple and inviting anyone who knew a legal impediment to their marriage to speak up. The public nature of banns — anyone in the congregation could object — is exactly what makes Petruchio's absence scandalous: the community has been assembled, the contract publicly declared, and the groom has not appeared.

Petruchio invokes the convention for comic deflation: the wedding guests gaping at his rags are, in his framing, merely beholders of a celestial wonder, not judges of a social transgression.

It is also a restatement of Elizabethan social theory about identity residing in the person, not the outward show.

anchor_text: seal the title with a lovely kiss
summary: Petruchio frames his first kiss with Katherina in legal property terms: to 'seal' a document was to press a wax seal onto it, converting a mere written agreement into a binding legal instrument. 'Title' here means legal ownership, as in a title-deed. He is claiming Katherina as property and the kiss as the act that ratifies that claim — the transaction language deliberately echoes the mercantile marriage negotiations of Act 2.
detail: The legal metaphor runs deep in the Taming subplot: Baptista negotiates Katherina's marriage as a financial transaction, Petruchio talks of his wife as 'my goods, my chattels' (1542), and Lucentio needs a substitute 'Vincentio' to 'make assurance here in Padua / Of greater sums.' A seal on a deed was the formal completion of a legal transfer; the kiss-as-seal trope conflates love with ownership in a single pun. The same legal-erotic conceit appears in Sonnet 120's 'The humble salve which wounded bosoms fits' and in numerous Elizabethan love lyrics.

anchor_text: 'Ay, by gogs-wouns' quoth he
summary: 'Gogs-wouns' is a minced oath — a softened, disguised form of 'God's wounds,' referring to the wounds of Christ on the cross. Such oaths were common in Elizabethan England; an Act of Parliament in 1606 (the Act to Restrain Abuses of Players) prohibited the use of the actual divine name on stage, which is why dramatists used these distorted forms. Swearing such an oath loudly enough to startle a priest shows spectacular impiety at the holiest moment of the wedding ceremony.
detail: The 1606 Act required substitution of 'God' with softer alternatives ('Jove,' 'gog,' 'faith,' etc.); some of these minced forms predated the statute and were simply habitual hedges. 'Gogs-wouns' blends 'God's' (softened to 'gog's') and 'wounds' (softened to 'wouns'). Petruchio's delivery of this oath at the precise moment the priest poses the consent question — 'if Katherine should be his wife' — is the scene's central outrage: he swears rather than answers, and so violently that the priest drops the Book of Common Prayer.

anchor_text: Carouse full measure to her maidenhead
summary: To 'carouse' is to drink a full, deep draught without stopping. 'Maidenhead' (maidenhood, virginity) is the ostensible object of the drinking toast, but the phrasing makes it a bawdy double entendre: Petruchio invites the guests to drink deeply in honor of a virginity that will very soon cease to exist, since he is about to take it. Petruchio's version is especially brutal: he tells the guests to drink the toast and then denies the bride the dinner she would normally share with them, hauling her off before any of the usual wedding festivities. 'Carouse' comes from the German 'gar aus' (entirely out, emptying the cup); a full carousal was a serious pledge of a full drink.

anchor_text: She is my goods, my chattels; she is my house, My household stuff, my field, my barn, My horse, my ox, my ass, my anything
summary: Petruchio lists Katherina as his legal property. Under the Elizabethan doctrine of 'coverture,' derived from common law, a wife had no independent legal identity: upon marriage all her property and her legal person were subsumed into her husband's. A husband could not 'rob' his own wife any more than he could rob his own furniture. Petruchio is not merely being rude — he is stating the law of England.
detail: Coverture (from the French 'couverture,' cover) meant that a married woman (a 'feme covert') had no right to own property, enter contracts, or sue in her own name; she was legally invisible, folded into her husband's legal identity. Petruchio's items — goods, chattels, house, household stuff, field, barn, horse, ox, ass — escalate from movable personal property (chattels), to real estate, to livestock, all of which were under the husband's absolute control. The doctrine remained largely in force in England until the Married Women's Property Act of 1870 (and further reforms in 1882). Annotate this as a structural truth of the play, not a character flaw unique to Petruchio: the play dramatizes what the law permitted.

anchor_text: My horse, my ox, my ass, my anything
summary: Petruchio's list of possessions — house, field, horse, ox, ass — matches almost exactly the items listed in the Tenth Commandment's prohibition on coveting a neighbour's property: 'Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house... nor his servant, nor his maid, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's' (Exodus 20:17). An Elizabethan audience steeped in the Bible and the Catechism would catch the echo at once, and the comedy is sharp: Petruchio is using the property-list that the commandment forbids coveting as proof of his own ownership.

Petruchio inverts the commandment's meaning: where the Bible warns others not to covet his goods, he is warning others not to steal them — the same list, the same logic of exclusive ownership, but asserted rather than protected. That the wife appears first ('his wife') in the commandment and that Petruchio includes her in the same breath as horse and ox was, for Elizabethan readers, theologically accurate rather than satirically exaggerated.

summary: To 'buckler' someone means to shield or defend them, from the buckler — a small round shield, typically 9-18 inches across, held in the fist or strapped to the forearm. anchor_text: cum privilegio ad imprimendum solum

The joke links the world of Elizabethan publishing monopolies to marriage, treating Bianca as a text to be owned exclusively.

anchor_text: I knew a wench married in an afternoon as she went to the garden for parsley to stuff a rabbit
summary: Biondello's comic anecdote captures the Elizabethan reality of the clandestine marriage: a couple could marry with almost no preparation so long as a priest, a clerk, and two witnesses were at hand. Going to the garden for parsley — a domestic errand — is Biondello's way of saying the elopement need take no longer than a routine chore. His point to Lucentio: stop hesitating and go now, while Baptista is safely distracted at Tranio's lodging.

Clandestine marriages — performed without banns, sometimes in private houses — were technically irregular but valid if uncontested, and common enough to fuel repeated attempts at ecclesiastical reform. The Fleet Prison 'irregular' marriages of the seventeenth century are the best-known product of this laxity. The priest of Saint Luke's, ready 'at all hours,' is this play's version of such a compliant cleric.

summary: Petruchio swears an oath by 'my mother's son' — a roundabout way of saying 'by myself,' since he is his mother's son. Katherina's willingness to accept even this extreme substitution marks the pivot of the scene: she is no longer resisting Petruchio's game, she is playing it — and doing so with a certain sardonic flair.

anchor_text: the moon changes even as your mind
summary: Katherina's yielding is not simple capitulation: she slips in a pointed comparison between the moon and Petruchio's mind, both equally changeable. The phrase 'And so it shall be so for Katherine' confirms her compliance — but the line about the changing moon quietly preserves her intelligence even as she surrenders the argument. Editors note this as the scene's dramatic fulcrum.

Juliet swears by the moon and Romeo warns her it is 'too inconstant' (Romeo and Juliet 2.2). Here Katherina turns that commonplace against Petruchio: if the sky-light changes with his mind, then it might as well be the moon. The concession she offers in the next line ('What you will have it named, even that it is') is strategically total — she grants him the power to name reality — while the moon-mind comparison preserves the verbal sting. Whether Katherina is genuinely broken, shrewdly choosing her battles, or playing a long game is the interpretive crux of the whole play, and this speech is its best evidence.

anchor_text: thus the bowl should run, And not unluckily against the bias
summary: Petruchio uses bowling to celebrate his victory in the sun/moon dispute. In the Elizabethan lawn game of bowls, the wooden ball (the 'bowl') was weighted on one side — its 'bias' — to make it curve; a bowl that ran 'against the bias' curved the wrong way and went wide. Petruchio is saying the game has finally run as it should: Katherina, like a well-biased bowl, has followed the intended line.

The bias — the weighted insert that made the bowl curve — was also a byword for a natural inclination or tendency; to act 'against the bias' was to go contrary to one's nature or purpose (compare Richard II 3.4: 'the world is set against the bias'). Petruchio's image is smugly confident, but it also implies that Katherina's compliance is now her natural direction of travel — which the audience may or may not believe.

anchor_text: Such war of white and red within her cheeks
summary: Petruchio deliberately praises old Vincentio as if he were a beautiful young woman — the 'war of white and red within her cheeks' refers to the blazon (formal praise-poem) convention in which a woman's complexion was described as a battle between the pallor of white and the bloom of red. The more absurd the praise lands on an elderly man, the more it tests Katherina's willingness to play along.

Sidney's Astrophil and Stella and many other sonnet sequences use it straight; Shakespeare parodies it in Sonnet 130 ('My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun'). The blazon — a catalogue of a beloved's physical beauties — was the default mode of Elizabethan love-poetry, and Petruchio delivers a complete one to an old man in travelling clothes. The device is a deliberate public test of Katherina: she must either correct him (reverting to her old defiance) or embrace the fiction, which is what she does in the speech that follows.

anchor_text: Young budding virgin, fair and fresh and sweet
summary: Katherina now addresses the old man Vincentio in precisely the terms Petruchio used — calling him a 'young budding virgin' and fantasizing about the happy husband who will share his 'lovely bed-fellow.' She has not merely yielded; she has adopted Petruchio's own comic strategy and performs it with gusto. The speech is remarkable: scholars disagree whether it shows defeat, adaptation, or the beginnings of an equal partnership in the game.

Some productions play this as sarcastic, others as genuinely playful; the text supports both. The scene's dramaturgy is important: by having Petruchio immediately correct her ('This is a man, old, wrinkled, faded, wither'd'), the play frames the episode as a joint improvisation whose rules Petruchio controls but which Katherina has entered willingly. The episode structurally mirrors the sun/moon exchange — Petruchio sets the fiction, Katherina adopts it, he collapses it, she corrects herself — but here her performance is far more inventive than mere compliance.

anchor_text: if she be froward, Then hast thou taught Hortensio to be untoward
summary: 'Froward' means stubbornly contrary or difficult to manage — the exact word used of Katherina throughout the play. 'Untoward' means unruly, refractory, or unmanageable in the same sense. Hortensio intends to apply Petruchio's method to his widow: if she proves froward, he will be equally untoward in return. The paired antonyms frame the taming-school lesson as a strategy of matching stubbornness with stubbornness.

The closing couplet neatly summarises the play's central thesis as Hortensio understands it: Petruchio has demonstrated a technique, and Hortensio plans to copy it. anchor_text: I'll venture so much of my hawk or hound
summary: Petruchio scoffs at twenty crowns as a trivial wager — he would risk that on a hawk or a hound, let alone his wife. He then raises the wager to a hundred crowns — five times the starting bid.

To say twenty crowns is only worth a hawk or hound frames Petruchio's confidence as extravagant. Petruchio's confidence is, of course, vindicated, while the two men who were certain of their 'sweet' wives are embarrassed.

anchor_text: Katherine, that cap of yours becomes you not: Off with that bauble, throw it underfoot
summary: Petruchio orders Katherina to remove and destroy her cap in front of the assembled company. A woman's cap was a marker of social status and feminine propriety in the period — the same point of contention as in the haberdasher scene (4.3) where Petruchio rejected the fashionable cap Katherina wanted. The destruction of a piece of dress before witnesses signals her willingness to put his will above her own public presentation.

Now she removes and tramples a cap (presumably a different or the same type) before an audience without protest. The gesture makes the behavioral transformation visible and public, and the Widow's horrified 'Lord, let me never have a cause to sigh / Till I be brought to such a silly pass!' shows that the audience within the play reads it as degradation.

anchor_text: thy lord, thy king, thy governor
summary: The ascending triad — lord, king, governor — maps the husband's authority over his wife onto the political structure of the state: as a subject owes obedience to a lord, as a citizen owes it to a king, so a wife owes it to her husband. This was the standard patriarchal doctrine of Elizabethan domestic conduct manuals, sermons, and homilies. Katherina's speech draws directly on this official ideology, which Shakespeare presents without approval or disapproval: the play lets it stand as culturally real.
detail: The analogy of marriage to political sovereignty was explicit in Elizabethan doctrine. The official 'Homily on the State of Matrimony' (Homilies, 1563), read in every parish church, instructed that a wife owed her husband obedience as a subject owes a prince — virtually the exact terms of Katherina's speech. The triad 'lord / king / governor' runs from the personal to the political, making the husband a small-scale sovereign within the household. Modern readings of this speech debate whether Katherina voices genuine conviction, irony, or a tactical performance; nothing in the staging resolves the question, and productions have read it every way.

anchor_text: A woman mov'd is like a fountain troubled, Muddy, ill-seeming, thick, bereft of beauty
summary: This is an extended simile (the formal term is 'similitudo'): an angry woman is like a stirred-up spring — cloudy, thick, ugly, and unfit to drink from. The image works on two levels: literal (no one will drink from a muddy fountain) and social (no one will approach or value an angry woman). The point is tactical: anger destroys its own possessor, not the target.
detail: The simile draws on a natural commonplace — a spring or well that is clear when undisturbed but turbid when stirred — and applies it as a behavioral argument: Katherina is essentially telling the Widow and Bianca that anger is self-defeating vanity, since it destroys the angry person's own worth. The rhetorical move is to shift from moralizing to pragmatic self-interest: it is not just wrong to be angry, it is ugly and self-sabotaging. Whether this represents Katherina's genuine conversion or a learned-from-necessity performance is the interpretive crux of the speech.

anchor_text: Such duty as the subject owes the prince, Even such a woman oweth to her husband
summary: Katherina makes explicit the political analogy that runs through her speech: a wife's duty to her husband is identical in kind to a subject's duty to the monarch — total, unconditional, non-negotiable. A wife who defies her husband is therefore not merely unpleasant but a 'foul contending rebel / And graceless traitor' — criminal vocabulary from the law of treason, applied to the domestic sphere.
detail: The sovereign-subject / husband-wife analogy had genuine Elizabethan legal and theological weight. The homily literature, the conduct-book tradition (e.g. Juan Luis Vives, Instruction of a Christian Woman, trans. Hyrde 1529; Thomas Becon, The Boke of Matrimony, 1564), and Elizabethan canon law all employed exactly this parallel. To call a disobedient wife a 'rebel' and 'traitor' was to invoke the vocabulary of high treason — the most serious crime in the English legal system. Katherina's speech thus brings the full ideological weight of the Elizabethan state to bear on the question of wifely obedience; it is the most politically explicit statement of the play's central argument, and the most contested by modern readers and performers.

Katherina is now applying to the Widow and Bianca the same dismissive vocabulary that was once used about her.

anchor_text: Then vail your stomachs, for it is no boot, And place your hands below your husband's foot
summary: 'Vail your stomachs' means lower your pride — 'stomach' in the period meant arrogance, spirit, or temper, not the digestive organ. 'It is no boot' means there is no benefit (no 'good') in resisting. The physical gesture — placing one's hand beneath the husband's foot in token of submission — is a stylized act of feudal homage, offering to put oneself literally under his foot as a servant to a lord.
detail: The 'stomach' as the seat of pride, anger, and personal spirit is well-attested (OED, n., sense 6c). 'Boot' as 'benefit, use, advantage' is an archaism even in Shakespeare's time (OED, boot n.1, sense 2). The foot-gesture brings the speech to a physical crescendo: Katherina offers to put her hand beneath Petruchio's foot as a sign of submission. The gesture echoes the feudal practice of placing one's neck under a conqueror's boot, but rendered as voluntary hand-submission. In the play's staging Petruchio stops her — 'Come on, and kiss me, Kate' — before the gesture is completed, which some productions read as sentimentality, others as the play sidestepping the full humiliation.

anchor_text: Why, there's a wench! Come on, and kiss me, Kate
summary: Petruchio's response to Katherina's long speech is a public kiss — not a word of acknowledgment of her argument, just physical approval ('there's a wench'). 'Wench' could be affectionate (a spirited girl) or dismissive (a servant-woman); in context it is approbatory, a term of rough endearment from a social superior. The scene ends not with a conversation about obedience but with a display of it, and the closing action rewards the speech with a kiss rather than a reply.
detail: The play-within-a-play frame means this kiss is also the end of the entertainment Sly was meant to watch — though the Folio text has quietly dropped Sly by this point and never brings him back. The critical debate about Katherina's speech hangs partly on this moment: Petruchio asks for and receives the public kiss as the seal of his wager-win, and the scene's final couplets ('you two are sped,' 'I won the wager... though you hit the white') make clear that for Petruchio the goal has been the material and social victory, not an interior conversion. Whether Katherina shares in the victory or is its object is the question the play refuses to answer.

anchor_text: though you hit the white; And being a winner, God give you good night!
summary: 'Hit the white' is an archery term for hitting the white central ring of a target — equivalent to a modern bullseye. But 'Bianca' means 'white' in Italian, so Petruchio is saying Lucentio hit Bianca (married the beautiful girl) while Petruchio — the winner — won the larger prize: a truly obedient wife. The pun caps the whole play's plot.
detail: Archery targets had concentric rings of different colours; the 'white' or 'clout' was the innermost. Bianca's name transparently means 'white' or 'fair' in Italian (it is used decorously throughout the play as a byword for her outward sweetness and fairness), so the archery pun works as a retrospective joke on the whole Padua plot: Lucentio, Gremio, and Hortensio all aimed at the beautiful girl, but the real test of marital success — the wager — has been won by the man who aimed at the 'difficult' target. The wordplay on Bianca's name also gently undercuts her, since the bride who failed the obedience test is the one whose very name signals the 'bullseye' everyone else was shooting for.

anchor_text: thou hast tam'd a curst shrew
summary: 'Curst' means bad-tempered, sharp, shrewish — the standard Elizabethan word for the quality the play is named after. A 'shrew' was a scolding, quarrelsome woman; the word's literal sense (a small, fierce, sharp-toothed rodent) gave it its figurative force. The play ends by naming its own subject, and Lucentio's final half-line — ''Tis a wonder, by your leave, she will be tam'd so' — leaves the question open: it is a wonder, possibly a suspicious one.
